bibliographic.title: Don't blame me: How Intelligent Support Affects Moral Responsibility in Human Oversight
bibliographic.authors: Cedric Faas, Richard Uth, Sarah Sterz, Markus Langer, Anna Maria Feit
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the ACM Intelligent User Interfaces
bibliographic.citation_apa: Faas, C., Uth, R., Sterz, S., Langer, M., & Feit, A. M. (2026). Don't blame me: How intelligent support affects moral responsibility in human oversight. In Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces.

methodology.study_design: simulated oversight experiment with four between-subject conditions varying the number of intervention options (six, four, two, or one)
methodology.sample_description: participants who monitored an autonomous drone facing ten critical situations in a simulated oversight task
methodology.technology_context: AI decision support system that constrains overseer intervention choices during simulated autonomous drone monitoring in safety-critical scenarios

eligibility.decision_rationale: The study provides empirical evidence on how intelligent decision support that restricts intervention options affects perceived moral responsibility in human oversight of autonomous AI in safety-critical settings, with partial regulatory relevance (EU AI Act). However, the evaluated system is generic AI decision support in a drone simulation, not an LLM-based or conversational system; generative AI appears only in author acknowledgments for grammar checking.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Python metadata misidentified title/authors; scope fit for LLM conversational governance review requires human confirmation because governance themes are strong but technology context is non-conversational and non-LLM.

appraisal.notes: Clear experimental objective and adequate sample size are evident. Provided text offers limited detail on statistical analysis procedures and ethics procedures. Findings are clearly stated for the primary responsibility outcome, with acknowledged design trade-offs between safety restriction and meaningful human choice.

cerqual.explanation: Moderate confidence for claims about perceived moral responsibility under choice-restricting oversight support in simulated high-stakes settings. Relevance to the review's LLM conversational governance focus is limited because the study concerns non-conversational AI decision support in a drone oversight simulation.

coding.theme: Human oversight and moral responsibility under intelligent decision support
coding.subtheme: Effects of restricting overseer intervention options

synthesis.main_claim: When intelligent support restricts overseers to a single intervention option, overseers feel less morally responsible after a crash, while perceived responsibility of the AI and its developer does not change across restriction conditions.
synthesis.contribution: Offers empirical evidence and design guidance for oversight architectures: avoid attributing moral agency to AI, clarify distributed moral responsibility, and preserve epistemic and causal conditions needed for genuine human responsibility when preventing ethically undesirable outcomes.
synthesis.limitations: Performance improvements were detected only when no meaningful choice remained, raising whether human oversight should be required when safety-oriented interaction design undermines responsibility without meaningful human benefit; simulated setting may limit external validity.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as supporting evidence on human oversight, moral responsibility, and oversight UI/architecture design in regulated high-stakes AI contexts; not usable as central evidence on conversational LLM governance, guardrails, RAG, observability, or operational technical governance.

evidence.claim: Study investigates how choice-restricting decision support affects overseer moral responsibility when support errs
evidence.excerpt: The goal of our study was to investigate how a decision support system that restricted available interventions would affect overseer's perceived moral responsibility, in particular in cases where the support errs.

evidence.claim: Empirical between-subjects oversight experiment with N=274
evidence.excerpt: In a simulated oversight experiment, participants (N=274) monitored an autonomous drone that faced ten critical situations

evidence.claim: Single-option restriction reduces overseer perceived moral responsibility after crash
evidence.excerpt: participants, who were restricted to choosing from a single action, felt less morally responsible if a crash occurred

evidence.claim: Responsibility attributions to AI and developer unchanged across conditions
evidence.excerpt: participants' judgments about the responsibility of other stakeholders (the AI; the developer of the AI) did not change between conditions

evidence.claim: Oversight architectures should support epistemic and causal conditions for moral responsibility
evidence.excerpt: they should prevent users from attributing moral agency to AI, help them understand how moral responsibility is distributed

evidence.claim: Human oversight required in safety-critical tasks to mitigate risk and ensure responsibility
evidence.excerpt: In such safety-critical tasks, human oversight of the system is required to mitigate risk by ensuring responsibility and preserving human judgment

evidence.claim: Moral responsibility linked to epistemic and causal conditions for overseers
evidence.excerpt: to be morally responsible, overseers must satisfy both an epistemic condition (understanding why the drone crashes and how it could have been prevented) and a causal condition

evidence.claim: High-stakes context motivates safety restrictions on overseer choice
evidence.excerpt: However, in high-stakes scenarios, improving cognitive factors might not be enough.

evidence.claim: Human oversight may be questionable when design removes meaningful choice without benefit
evidence.excerpt: This raises the question of whether human oversight should be required when safety-oriented interaction designs undermine overseers' responsibility without meaningfully benefiting from human involvement.
